Shimmer Cloud · a swell before the dry, and long tails · study

In before the sound, and long after it

The cloud now arrives before the sound it belongs to and hangs long after it. Both come from the prism's own timing: the tail is the loop run forward, and the swell is the same loop run backward in time. Dry and wet are mixed the way a reverb is heard, and every take is levelled alike. Nothing plays until you click, one take at a time.

Where we left it

The phrase, then October's fifth-then-cloud: one jump at the door, eight trips through the prism. It hangs about two seconds and starts when the words start. The plan's next step asks for two things it can't do: arrive before the sound, and hang much longer.

The long tail

The same loop with no jump, run twice as long and kept louder: sixteen trips, each through a fresh cloud of 600 lenses, losing a little top every time, so the tail darkens as it hangs.

the phrase, long tail
Hangs 5.7 s past the words, to −30 dB.
your ear

The swell before the dry

The same lens run backward in time. Every delay the prism makes becomes an advance, so the cloud arrives before the words and crescendos into them. Nobody drew that crescendo: run backward, the loop's quietest pass comes first and its loudest last. Struck with a click, the swell reaches 1.8 s ahead.

A · the swell alone
Two seconds of lead, then the dry, no tail.
B · swell and tail
The whole shape: in before the words, out 5.7 s after.
your ear

Which light comes first in the swell

Highs first: the swell falls from hiss into the body of the voice (a click's highs centre 0.46 s ahead, its lows 0.25 s). Or turned around, lows first, the swell rising into the voice from underneath.

The same take as B above.
B · lows first
Same tail; only the swell's prism turned round.

On something struck

Speech hides the swell inside its own words. A struck chord (C, G, E, B, plain additive piano-ish tones) has one sharp onset, so the swell has one place to lead into.

How it works

A prism lens delays each frequency by its own amount and never makes anything louder. Run backward in time, each delay becomes an advance. So the swell is the tail's loop run in reverse: five short trips through the prism, faded so the farthest is quietest. Forward, the same loop runs sixteen trips and keeps more each time.

lead = reverse( loop( reverse(dry) ) ); tail = loop(dry); out = lead + dry + tail, the dry delayed by the lead(the swell) = the loop, run on the sound backward, then turned the right way round; (the tail) = the loop run forward; (what you hear) = swell, then the dry, then the tail

Measured with one click (it has no words of its own to bias the timing): the swell reaches 1.8 s ahead and rises steadily, -1.50s before: -18 dB · -1.00s before: -12 dB · -0.50s before: -2 dB · -0.20s before: -1 dB · -0.05s before: -10 dB. The tail falls 30 dB in 6.4 s and 45 dB in 8.2 s.

What it costs, live. A swell before a sound has to hear the sound first. Here that's free. Live, the dry has to wait the swell's length (two seconds here). That's fine on a playback track with delay compensation, or in a looper, and impossible on a mic you're monitoring. The live cloud should carry the swell as a lookahead knob and say so on its face.
